quote: தன்னைச் செய்தவர்க்கு அவர் நினைத்த தேயத்துச் சென்று பகை என்னும் இருளைக் கெடுக்கும்.

position: The darkness is enmity, and a wealthy king's command runs wherever he intends.
quote: அரசன் பொரு ளுடையனானால், தான் கருதிய தேசமெல்லாம் தன்னாணை நடத்துவானென்றது.

position: The darkness is ordinary suffering, which money in hand drives away anywhere one goes.
quote: இருள் என்னும் துன்பத்தைத் துரத்தி விட முடிகிறது.

position: Coming with grace and love means, for a king, taxing no more than the rightful one-sixth.
quote: அவற்றொடு கூடி வருதலாவது, ஆறிலொன்றாய் வருதல்.

position: It applies to any earner: not profiting from others' distress and not losing affection for one's intimates while earning.
quote: பொருள் தேடுங்கால் பிறர் வருத்தத்திற்கு உபகரியாதும், பயின்றார் மாட்டுக் காதலில்லாமலும்

position: உறுபொருள் is ownerless wealth: long-buried treasure and estates without heirs.
quote: வைத்தார் இறந்துபோக நெடுங்காலம் நிலத்தின்கண் கிடந்து பின் கண்டெடுத்தூஉம், தாயத்தார் பெறாததூஉமாம்.

position: உறுபொருள் is revenue connected with protection.
quote: உறு பொருள் - காவற் பொருள்.

note: Both make exclusive claims with the same structure. 400 says learning is true wealth and all others are not. 751 says nothing but wealth is anything. The Kural lets each chapter speak in absolutes.

Both use பொய்யா விளக்கு. In 299 the unfailing lamp of the wise is truthfulness and all other lamps are no lamps. Here the same phrase names money. Whether this is a deliberate reversal can't be proved, but the two verses compete for one title.
660 likens wealth made by deceit to water stored in an unfired pot, and Parimelazhagar brings that very image into his comment on 755 to explain why such wealth destroys its maker.
241 ranks grace far above material wealth, which even the base have. 757 makes material wealth the nurse that raises grace. The ranking stands but the independence doesn't.

Two elephant images for getting a task done without personally bearing the risk. In 678 one elephant is used to catch another, and in 758 the owner watches elephants fight. Both separate the one who directs from the danger.

39 says only what flows from virtue is pleasure, so virtue is the source. 760 makes rightly made wealth the ground from which virtue and pleasure both come easily. The order of the three aims differs by book.

position: தேற்றம் is being trusted by the king.
quote: அரசனால் தேறப்படுதலும்

position: தேற்றம் is the army's own clarity, and the good path is steadiness in fighting.
quote: நல்லவழிச்சேறலாவது மறஞ் செய்யுங் காலத்துக் கலக்கமின்மை.

position: It is winning the trust of the leader, close to Parimelazhagar but placed on the leader.
quote: தலைவனின் நம்பிக்கையைப் பெறுதல்

position: தார் is the enemy's vanguard, held off before pressing forward.
quote: அவர் தூசியைத் தன்மேல் வாராமல் தடுத்துத்தான் அதன்மேற்செல்வதே படையாவது.

position: தார் is the garland of victory that the capable army carries.
quote: வெற்றி மாலை தாங்கிச் செல்லக்கூடிய சிறந்த படையாகும்.

position: Display gives some standing, though the wording itself shows striking power and endurance remain indispensable.
quote: 'இல்லெனினும்' எனவே, அவற்றது இன்றியமையாமை பெறப்பட்டது.

position: The army's parade appearance should be more distinguished than either valour or endurance.
quote: இரண்டையும் விட ஒரு படையின் அணிவகுப்புத் தோற்றம் சிறப்புடையதாக

note: The same formula for two wealths: an army is தலை among a king's riches and listening is தலை among a person's. The phrase shows that 'chief of wealth' is relative to whose life is being described.
763 mocks the sea-roar of an army without heroes. 768 allows that an army without fight can still gain stature through its show. Noise is nothing in one and display is something in the other.

Two ways of confronting Death personified. In 269 ascetic power may leap past கூற்றம், and in 765 an army stands against it together. The renouncer escapes and the soldier faces, and only one of them needs others.

position: The spear is thrown at the man, and giving way means ending the glare by blinking.
quote: அவர் வேலைக்கொண்டு எறிய அஃது ஆற்றாது அந்நோக்கை அழித்து இமைக்குமாயின்

position: The spear is thrust into the eye itself, and blinking again at that is equal to defeat.
quote: மாற்றாரோடு எதிர்த்துச் சிவந்து நோக்கின கண்ணிலே ஒரு வேலினாலே எறிய

position: They press on to battle even if the king angrily forbids it, because their ardour doesn't diminish.
quote: தம் இறைவன் அது வேண்டா என்று முனியினும் அவ் வீரமிகுதி குன்றார்.

position: The true warriors are those who go on doing their duty though their leader is angry with them.
quote: தலைவன் சினந்தாலும் சிறப்புக் குறையாமல் கடமை ஆற்றுபவர்கள்தான்

note: Both use பேராண்மை. Here the word is first attached to fierceness in battle. In 148 the great manhood is not looking at another's wife. The Kural contests what manhood is, and 773's own turn to helping the fallen foe is partway to 148.

Two claims about the sharpest edge (எஃகு). In 759 wealth is the sharpest steel for cutting an enemy's pride. In 773 the edge of valour is helping that enemy when he falls. Cutting and sparing are both called sharpness.

596 says aim high, since even a failure is as good as not failing. 772 gives the warrior's version: the spear that missed an elephant is better than the arrow that hit a hare. Aim outranks outcome in both.

Both judge a life day by day and ask for no wasted days. In 38 the good deed makes a day count, and it blocks future births. In 776 the wound makes a day count. Two complete moral accountings use one form.

1066 says nothing shames the tongue more than begging, even water for a cow. 780 says this death is worth begging for, with the same root (இர-). Only something beyond the Kural's worst disgrace could justify the word.
231 says the only profit for a life is to give and live with fame (இசை). 777 wants the same இசை, and pays for it with life itself. Giving and dying are two routes to one reward.

position: Nayam is delight: both friendship and study give increasing pleasure.
quote: நூற் பொருள் கற்குந்தோறும் கற்றார்க்கு இன்பஞ் செய்தலை ஒக்கும்.

position: The gain is understanding: a friend of good character teaches as a book does.
quote: இது குணவானோடு நட்புக் கொள்ளின், அறிவுண்டா மென்றது.

note: 448 says a king with no one to rebuke him falls even without enemies. 784 makes the same office of rebuke the very purpose of friendship. What a counsellor does for a ruler, a friend does for anyone.

783 says friendship grows with practice and 785 says practice isn't needed. Parimelazhagar reconciles them by ranking three causes of friendship and placing shared feeling first, but the verses themselves sit in plain tension.

785 makes acquaintance unnecessary, while a whole chapter on old friendship opens at 801. Parimelazhagar's gloss on 801 eases this by saying that பழைமை is not elapsed time but a certain kind of friendship.

Both liken a relationship to learning with a 'the more, the more' (-தொறும்). In 783 friendship deepens like study's delight, and in 1110 love with the beloved is like finding one's ignorance with each new thing learned. Learning gives the Kural its model of an inexhaustible bond.

position: குன்றா இனன் is a friend's undiminished kin, since those bound to kin bring that bond along with them.
quote: சுற்றப் பிணிப்புடையார் நட்டாரோடும் பிணிப்புண்டு வருதலின்

position: The phrase means qualities that don't decline, not relatives.
quote: குறையாத இயல்புகள் எவை?

position: The verse describes friends, who dissuade before the act, press hard after it, and make one do what is proper.
quote: தாம் உலக வழக்கல்லது செய்யக் கருதின்சோகம் பிறக்கும்வகை சொல்லி விலக்கியும்

position: The verse is about which ministers a ruler should befriend.
quote: இது மந்திரிகளுள் நட்பாக்கற் பாலாரைக் கூறிற்று.

position: ஒப்பிலார் are those out of accord with the world.
quote: உலகோடு ஒத்தலில்லார் நட்பினை அறியாது கொண்டாராயின்

position: ஒப்பிலார் are those not one's equals.
quote: தனக்கு நிகரில்லாதார் நட்பினின்று நீங்குக

position: They are simply those who carry a stain, the contrary of the first half.
quote: மாசு உள்ளவர்களின் நட்பை, விலைகொடுத்தாவது விலக்கிடவேண்டும்.

note: 791 demands inquiry before a friendship begins. 796 says ruin is what truly measures friends, and Manakkudavar adds it is hard to know them otherwise. So the test that matters most can't be run in advance, and this undercuts the chapter's own program.

791 says those devoted to friendship cannot leave a friend once made. 797 calls leaving a fool's friendship pure gain. Parimelazhagar's 800 offers a way out: leaving is for what one took on without knowing.

793 and 794 screen friends by family. 972 says birth is equal for all living beings and only deeds make the difference. The chapter on choosing friends keeps a criterion that the chapter on greatness dissolves.

position: The act is one's own business done for one by a friend unasked, and nothing is better than finding it done.
quote: ஒருவர்க்குத் தம் கருமம் தாம் அறியாமல் முடிந்திருத்தலின் ஊங்கு நன்மை யின்மையின்

position: The act is something one doesn't approve, and one should still welcome it and not only permit it.
quote: கேளாது இசைவில்லாதவற்றைச் செய்வாராயின், அதற்கு முனியாது

position: The day a friend lapses is a day of real worth, for it alone shows such intimacy.
quote: செய்து போந்துழியல்லது அவ்வுரிமை வெளிப்படாமையின், செய்யாதன நாளல்லவாயின.

position: Such a day is a good day.
quote: நட்டோர் தப்புச் செய்யின், அந்த நாள் நல்ல நாளாம்

position: The reverse: if they do wrong to one so trusting, all the days of that friendship were wasted.
quote: அவர்களுடன் நட்புக் கொண்டிருந்த நாளெல்லாம் வீணான நாளாகும்.

note: Salt in both, and both about intimacy that hurts a little. In 802 the worthy are salt to friendship's liberties, and in 1302 lovers' sulking is salt that spoils when overdone. 1302 supplies the measure 802 leaves out.

797 says dropping a fool's friendship is gain. 805 says when an old friend hurts you, consider it folly and go on. The same பேதைமை is a reason for leaving in one chapter and an excuse for staying in the next, and the only difference is how old the bond is.

800 says pay if you must to escape a bad friend. 807 says love does not end even when an old friend ruins you. Between them lies a question the Kural doesn't settle: at what point does a harmful friend stop being an old friend and become one you never should have made?

position: The small are base people in general, whose failure is that they leave in ruin.
quote: அரணாகாமை - தொலைவின்கண் விட்டு நீங்குதல்.

position: The small are particular kinds of people, gamblers, hunters and women among them, a gendered list which the verse doesn't contain.
quote: சிறியார் - சூதர், வேட்டைக் காரர், பெண்டிர் போல்வார்.

note: 784 says friendship exists to rebuke, openly and in advance. 818 says that with a certain kind of friend, say nothing and let it fade. Whether one rebukes turns out to depend on whether the friend is still worth the rebuke.
784 says friendship isn't for laughter. 817 raises that to a ten-crore disadvantage against enemies. A verse about purpose becomes a verdict on a whole class of companion.

911 says the women who desire wealth rather than the man bring ruin through sweet words. 813 applies the same logic to friends who calculate, and the comparison runs the other way: chapter 92's accusation is made first of men's friendships.

position: Women's minds are changeable once there is an opportunity, and he supports it from another text.
quote: இடம் பெற்றால் பெண்பாலார் மனம் போல வேறுபடும்.

position: The comparison concerns only prostitutes, who pretend to the virtue that women have, so women in general are not the target.
quote: நடிக்கும் விலை மகளிரின் மனம்போல உள்ளொன்றும் புறமொன்றுமாக

position: மாணார் are enemies, and learning won't make them friends, so don't trust them because they are learned.
quote: அதனான் மனம் திருந்தி நட்பாதல் பகைவர்க்கு இல்லை

position: மாணார் are simply those lacking excellence, and the point is about what learning can reveal.
quote: மனநல்லாராகு தல் மாட்சிமையில்லார்க்கு அரிது

note: 706 says the face shows what is in the heart as crystal shows what is beside it. 824 fears those whose face shows the reverse. Chapter 71 rests on the reliability of signs and chapter 83 on their failure, and Parimelazhagar's note on 824 calls the face the instrument of reading.
824 fears hostility that does not show. 826 says an enemy's fine words are soon seen through. The chapter holds two views on whether concealment can succeed.

279 says the straight arrow is cruel and the bent lute is kind, so judge by deed. 827 says the bent bow means harm. The two verses reach for the same geometry to make the same point, that shape doesn't reveal intent.
71 says love can't be locked in, and that tears publish it. 828 says an enemy's tears may hide a weapon. The evidence that the Book of Virtue trusts absolutely is, in the Book of Wealth, a cover.

34 says all virtue comes to a stainless mind and the rest is noise. 829 teaches outward friendship with inward death. Parimelazhagar accepts the conflict openly and resolves it as a rule for enemies only, which is a substantive claim about how the books of the Kural relate.
786 says friendship of the face alone is not friendship. 830 tells the reader to use just that kind on a suspect enemy (முகம் நட்டு). What is a failure in one chapter becomes a technique in another.

position: It means conduct forbidden by the treatises, loved and done anyway.
quote: இருமைக்கும் ஆகாதென்று நூலோர் கடிந்த செயல்களை விரும்பிச் செய்தல் என்பதாம்.

position: It means something out of reach, loved even though effort won't get it.
quote: தனக்குக் கைவாராத பொருளின்கண் காதன்மை செய்தல்

position: It means tasks beyond one's ability, and meddling in them.
quote: தன்னால் இயலாத செயல்களை விரும்பி, அவற்றில் தலையிடுவது

position: The mire is hell, and all future births are lived in hell's suffering because of one life's cruel deeds.
quote: வரும் பிறவிகள் எல்லாம் தான் புக்கு அழுந்தும் நிரயத்தினை

position: ஒருமை is acting on one's own whim, and எழுமை simply means always. The mire is suffering with no births or hell involved.
quote: எக் காலத்திலும் துன்பமெனும் சகதியில் அழுந்திக் கிடக்க நேரிடும்.

position: It is mock praise, blame dressed as praise: the friendship wanes daily, so parting hurts no one.
quote: புகழ்வார் போன்று பழித்தவாறு.

position: It concerns women's relations with foolish men, and how a fool enjoys desire.
quote: இது பேதை காமந் துய்க்குமாறு கூறிற்று.

position: He gives the literal sense, with no irony marked: it is sweet because parting brings no sorrow.
quote: பிரியும்போது எந்தத் துன்பமும் ஏற்படுவதில்லை.

note: A precise inversion using the same ஒருமை and எழுமை. In 398 learning gained in one birth protects for seven. In 835 folly done in one birth drowns for seven. One life's leverage on all the lives to come works in both directions.

823 says study doesn't reform the hostile. 834 turns the same point on the student and teacher himself: he is the worst fool. Learning fails as moral change in both, first in the other and then in oneself.
782 says a fool's friendship wanes like the moon. Parimelazhagar uses that waning to explain 839's joke: because it has been shrinking every day, by the time of parting nothing is left to hurt.

position: To cover a fault means to get rid of it. Covering the lesser thing while leaving the greater and thinking oneself decent is the folly.
quote: குற்றம் மறைத்தலாவது, அவற்றை இலவாக்குதல்.

position: To cover a fault means keeping it from others' notice, as clothing hides the body from view.
quote: தம்பாலுள்ள குற்றத்தைப் பிறரறியாமல் தாம் மறையாத காலத் து

position: மறை is rare teaching which the fool doesn't take in. He rejects the other reading explicitly, since leaking a secret would be carelessness and not this fault.
quote: அது பேணாமை என்னும் பேதைமையாவதன்றிப் புல்லறிவாண்மையன்மை அறிக.

position: மறை is a closely held secret, and letting it slip means telling others.
quote: சோரவிடுதல் - பிறர்க்குச் சொல்லுதல்.

position: What is denied is God, rebirth, and the fruit of deeds, as affirmed by the eminent.
quote: கடவுளும், மறுபிறப்பும், இருவினைப் பயனும் முதலாக அவர் உள என்பன பலவேனும்

position: What is denied is what the many wise affirm, with no specific doctrine named.
quote: உலகத்தில் அறிவுடையார் பலர் உண்டென்பதாகிய ஒரு பொருளை இல்லையென்று

position: What is denied is what's been shown clearly by evidence, and the denial is deliberate.
quote: ஆதாரங்களைக் காட்டி இதுதான் உண்மை என்று தெளிவாகக் கூறப்படுகிற ஒன்றை

note: Two reports of what the world does. 752 says everyone despises those with nothing. 841 says the world doesn't count lack of wealth as lack. Both can't be plain observation, so at least one of them is the Kural speaking for how the world ought to judge.

Same doubled form (இன்மையுள் இன்மை, இன்மையின் இன்மை). 1041 says the only thing as painful as poverty is poverty. 841 gives the title to lack of understanding. The chapter on poverty and this one rank the worst lack differently.

850 makes denying the world's consensus demonic. 423 says wisdom is finding the truth in anything, whoever says it. Parimelazhagar's doctrinal list sharpens this, and Kalaignar's 'evidence' moves 850 closer to 423.

Both are about the garment and the shame of exposure. In 788 a friend's help comes as fast as the hand to a slipping cloth. In 846 the cloth over the body is exposed as a fraud if faults stay bare. One makes the reflex an ideal and the other mocks it as a substitute.

position: The joy is worldly: with everyone a friend, one obtains every fruit.
quote: யாவரும் நட்பாகலின் எல்லாப் பயனும் எய்தியுறுவது.

position: The joy is liberation, the highest of all joys.
quote: எல்லா இன்பத்தின் மிக்க வீடுபேற்றின்பம் எய்தும் என்றவாறு.

position: மெய்ப்பொருள் here is the content of the treatises on policy, which brings success to those who follow them.
quote: வெற்றி பொருந்துதலையுடைய நீதி நூற்பொருளை அறியமாட்டார்.

position: It is truth as such, which those in conflict can't perceive.
quote: இது மாறுபடுவார்க்கு மெய்ப்பொருள் தோன்றாதென்றது.

note: Both tell the injured not to return harm, but their reasons differ. In 314 the wrongdoer is shamed by kindness. In 852, on Parimelazhagar's reading, one's own position is improved. The same act is justified in moral terms in one book and in terms of advantage in another.

829 tells one to answer hidden contempt with hidden death. 852 says not to return harm even to one who plans division. They are three chapters apart in the same stretch on friends and foes, and the Kural offers both as sound counsel.

Two kinds of invincibility, each put as 'don't attempt it'. 771's warrior warns that those who stood before his lord now stand as stones. 855's person is unbeatable because he leans away. One's strength is in striking and the other's in declining.

784 says friendship isn't for laughter (நகுதல்). 860 makes நகல் the very source of good ways, which Parimelazhagar glosses as friendship. The same root gets very different valuations in the chapter on what friendship is for and the chapter on hostility.

position: It is a plain rule of statecraft: avoid the strong, and keep enmity with the weak, since beating them doesn't drain one's strength.
quote: ஏனை மெலியார்க்குப் பகையாதலை ஒழியாது விரும்புக.

position: The weak in view are those who don't respect one, which narrows the rule.
quote: தம்மைப் போற்றாத எளியார்மாட்டுப் பகைகோடலை மேவுக

position: The opposite: true excellence in enmity is leaving the weak alone and taking on the strong.
quote: மெலியோரை விடுத்து, வலியோரை எதிர்த்துப் போரிட விரும்புவதே

position: வழி is the treatise on policy, handed down from the ancients, which he doesn't study.
quote: ஒருவன் நீதிநூலை ஓதான்

position: வழி is the consequence of an action, which he doesn't consider when he starts it.
quote: ஒருவினை செய்யத் தொடங்குங்கால் பின் வருவன பாரான்

position: He is a ruler who has begun a task and does what doesn't fit it, so losing a little to fight him pays many times over.
quote: வினையைத் தொடங்கியிருந்து அதற்கு ஏலாதன செய்வான் பகைமையை

position: He has taken up enmity and does what doesn't serve it, so he will not actually hurt you.
quote: இஃது இவன் பகைசெய்யமாட்டானாதலால், அப்பகை கோடலாமென்றது.

position: He is someone staying at your side and doing wrong, and you must pay to make him an open enemy.
quote: தன்னோடு இருந்துகொண்டே தனக்குப் பொருந்தாத காரியங்களைச் செய்து கொண்டிருப்பவனைப்

position: Fighting the untaught is cheap in effort, and one who can't manage even that won't win fame.
quote: நீதி அறியாதானை வேறல் எளிதாயிருக்கவும், அது மாட்டாதானை வெற்றியான் வரும் புகழ் கூடாது என்பதாம்

position: The words describe one enemy who is unlearned, angry and poor, and it is he whom light never reaches.
quote: கல்லாதானுமாய், வெகுளியுடையனுமாய், சிறு பொருளனுமாகிய பகைவனை எல்லா நாளும் ஒளி பொருந்தாது

note: The same two words, வலியார் and மெலியார், with opposite advice. 250 says that when going against the weak, remember how you stand before the strong, which is a brake. 861 tells a ruler to go against the weak with appetite. The Book of Virtue and the Book of Wealth are at their furthest apart here.

Two adjacent chapter openings. 861 tells one to keep enmity with the weak. 871 says enmity shouldn't be desired even in jest. Parimelazhagar's way through is that 871 is about unworthy enmity (மாணாத பகை), but the verses don't draw this distinction.

The same phrase, கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும். 794 says to pay for the friendship of a person of honour. 867 says to pay for the enmity of a fool. The Kural prices enemies and friends in the same way, and both are investments.

position: ஏமுற்றவர் are the mad, who at least aren't harmed by their delusion, while this one is.
quote: மயக்கத்தால் ஒப்பாராயினும் ஏமுற்றவர் அதனால் தீங்கு எய்தாமையின்

position: ஏமுற்றவர் are the arrogant, and this person is better called a fool than arrogant.
quote: ஆணவம் பிடித்தவன் என்பதைவிட அறிவிலி என்பதே பொருத்தமாகும்.

position: A king who, when it is needed, wins enemies over, and whose power therefore holds the world.
quote: வேண்டியவழிப் பகையை வேறுபடுத்துத் தனக்கு நட்பாகச் செய்து கொண்டொழுகும் இயல்பினையுடைய அரசனது

position: One able to behave toward enemies as if they were friends.
quote: பகைவரை நட்புபோலக் கொண்டொழுக வல்ல பண்புடையவன்

position: It is a moral nobility in anyone who thinks of enemies as friends, and the world praises it.
quote: பகைவர்களையும் நண்பர்களாகக் கருதிப் பழகுகின்ற பெருந்தன்மையான பண்பை

position: Their enemies will grow and destroy them, so they won't live even long enough to draw breath. He allows that it may be the enemy's breath that kills.
quote: அவர் உயிர்த்த துணையானே தாம் இறப்பர் எனினும் அமையும்.

position: It is the enemy's breath that kills, and the lesson is not to take on the strong as enemies at all.
quote: இது பகை கொள்ளுங்கால் வலியாரோடு பகைகோடலாகா தென்றது.

position: They can't be said to live merely because they are breathing.
quote: சுவாசிக்கிற காரணத்தினாலேயே, உயிரோடிருப்பதாக நிச்சயமாகச் சொல்ல முடியாது.

note: 874 says the world rests on the one who turns enemies into friends. 830 says that when an enemy turns friend, give only your face and drop even that later. If this is the same event seen from both sides, then each party in 874's triumph has reason to be following 830.

852 and its chapter say it is best not to return harm and to lean away from hostility. 879 says to kill the threat while it is young. One counsels letting enmity die by itself and the other warns that it won't, and both claim the outcome is self-preservation.

In 763 the rats die when the cobra merely breathes (உயிர்ப்ப). In 880 those who don't break a foe's pride don't survive his breath (on Manakkudavar's reading). The word for breathing is the unit of how little it takes.

Both warn against telling pain to those not attuned to it. In 877 it is a matter of strategy and self-respect, and in 1200 the lover scolds her own heart for telling sorrow to one who doesn't care. The advice carries across books, and it is much sadder in the second one.

position: It is about a king: an outwardly related enemy who may kill him, aid outside foes, and erode his ministers.
quote: புறப்பகைத் துணையாய் நின்றே அது தோன்றாமல் கோறல் முதலிய வஞ்சனை செய்தலும்

position: It is about enmity among close relatives in general, who all then suffer.
quote: நெருங்கிய உறவினருக்கிடையே தோன்றும் உட்பகையானது

position: The members look united but are not, and will split when an outside enemy comes. He notes other readings with the enmity itself as what doesn't join.
quote: உட்பகையான் மனம் வேறுபட்டமையின், புறப்பகை பெற்றுழி வீற்றுவீற்றாவர் என்பதாம்.

position: The enmity and the family are what fit together, and the lid moves aside for the one who comes to take what's inside, as the insider assists the thief.
quote: செப்பகத் துப் பொருள் வாங்குவார்க்கு மூடி துணையாய் அகன்று நிற்குமதுபோல அகன்று நிற்பரென்றவாறு.

position: பொன் is iron, the hard metal worn down by a file, and the insider seems to help while slowly separating people.
quote: அரத்தாற் பொரப்பட்ட இரும்பு போல அதனால் பொரப்பட்டு வலி தேயும்.

position: பொன் is gold, which is polished as it is filed. So inner enmity seems to beautify while it wastes strength.
quote: இஃது உட்பகை அழகு செய்வது போலப் பலத்தைக் கெடுக்கு மென்றது.

note: In 735 the land should be free from உட்பகை, which Parimelazhagar glosses as robbers, slanderers and even wild animals. In 881 the same commentator takes the word as kin. The term shrinks from a realm's internal troubles to a family's, and it hurts more in the smaller frame.

Both use a tiny seed against a huge effect. In 104 a millet-seed favour counts as large as a palmyra to those who understand it, and in 889 a sesame-seed enmity holds complete ruin. Small things turn out to be large in the Kural in both moral directions.

position: The great are ascetics, whose wrath strikes at the life itself in an instant where fire only reaches the body first.
quote: தவத்தாற் பெரியாரைப் பிழைத்து ஒழுகுவார், எவ்வாற்றானும் உயிருய்யார்.

position: The great are sages, with the same conclusion.
quote: இது முனிவரைப் பிழைத்தலினால் வருங்குற்றம் கூறிற்று.

position: The great are simply those mighty in capacity, with no asceticism involved.
quote: ஆற்றல் மிகுந்த பெரியோரிடம் தவறிழைப்போர் தப்பிப் பிழைப்பது முடியாது.

position: குன்ற மதித்தல் is what the hill-like ascetics do, resolving on someone's ruin, and the rich die with their kin at once.
quote: குன்றத்தை ஒக்கும் அருந்தவர் கெட நினைப்பாராயின்

position: It is done to them: someone thinks little of those who are great as hills.
quote: குன்ற மதித்தல் - அவமதித்தல்.

position: The வேந்தன் is Indra, himself toppled by ascetics of great vows, with Nahusha's fall from Indra's seat through Agastya's anger in mind.
quote: அவராற்றலான் இந்திரனும் இடைய தன் பதம் இழந்து கெடும்.

position: It is also Indra, who loses his realm, and this is a loss of wealth.
quote: உயர்ந்த கோட்பாட்டையுடையார் வெகுள்வராயின், இந்திரனும் இடையிலே இற்றுத் தன்னரசு இழக்கும்

position: Those with firm principles rise up and a repressive regime collapses, with no god or vow in it.
quote: அடக்குமுறை ஆட்சி நிலை குலைந்து அழிந்துவிடும்.

note: 781 says no guard is as hard to get past as friendship. 891 says not slighting the able outranks every safeguard. Parimelazhagar lists friendship among those it outranks, so a long section that praised friendship and forts closes by ranking something above them.

Death personified, twice. In 765 an army stands united when Death comes raging. In 894 the fool waves Death over with his own hand. The difference between courage and folly is not whether one faces Death, but whether one sent the invitation.

Both rank fire below something else: in 129 the burn from fire heals and the burn of the tongue doesn't, and in 896 one may survive the fire but not offence given to the great. Fire is the Kural's standard for what is bad but survivable.

29 calls the great those who have climbed a hill of virtue, whose anger can't be withstood even for a moment. 898 calls them hill-like, and 896-897 in Parimelazhagar's reading have the same instant destruction. Chapter 90 develops what chapter 3 states about the renunciant, in the political book.

25 calls Indra sufficient witness to the power of the one who controls the senses. Parimelazhagar makes 899's வேந்தன் Indra as well. The Kural itself only names Indra in 25, so the connection depends on his gloss.

864 says one who doesn't let go of anger is easy prey for anyone. 899 makes the anger of the exalted able to bring down a king. Anger is weakness or supreme power depending on who has it, and 306 warns that it burns the one who has it.

position: What he abandons is his manliness, and his wealth shames all men because she controls its use.
quote: தன் ஆண்மையை விட்டு மனையாளது பெண்மையை விழைவான்

position: What he fails to tend is virtue and wealth, with no appeal to manliness.
quote: அறத்தினையும் பொருளினையும் பேணாது மனையாளைக் காதலிப் பானது செல்வம்

position: What he neglects is the principle he adopted, as he trails after a woman.
quote: ஏற்றுக்கொண்ட கொள்கையினைப் பேணிக் காத்திடாமல்

position: The fault is a husband's fear of any wife: fear is natural to her, so in him it is unnatural and leaves her uncontrolled.
quote: அவள் தான் அஞ்சி ஒழுகுதல் இயல்பாகலின், அவளை அஞ்சுதல் இயல்பின்மையாயிற்று.

position: The fault is yielding to a wife of bad character instead of trying to correct her.
quote: நற்குணமில்லாத மனைவியைத் திருத்த முனையாமல் பணிந்து போகிற கணவன்

position: மறுமை is the next world, whose fruit he forfeits because he cannot perform household virtue.
quote: தன் மனையாளை அஞ்சி ஒழுகுகின்ற மறுமைப்பயன் இல்லாதானுக்கு

position: The man fears running a family and misses the fruit of the new life that marriage opens; no next world is involved.
quote: மணம் புரிந்து புதுவாழ்வின் பயனை அடையாமல் குடும்பம் நடத்த அஞ்சுகின்றவனின்

position: He fears giving to guests, ascetics and elders, even out of wealth he earned himself.
quote: தான் தேடிய பொருளே யாயினும் அதனால் நல்லார்க்கு நல்லன செய்தலை

position: He reverses the sense: a man anxious to do good without error heeds the wife who watches for error.
quote: தவறு நேராமல் கண்காணிக்கும் மனைவிக்கு அஞ்சி நடப்பான்.

note: Both set a wife's or beloved's shoulders against heaven. 906 says that fearing those shoulders leaves no worth even in a godlike life, and 1103 asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep on them. Fear and love differ, but the books value the same intimacy in opposite ways.

Both redefine manliness away from dominance over others. 148 gives பேராண்மை to the man who doesn't look at another's wife, and 907 finds the opposite failure in a man who takes a woman's orders: in each case ஆண்மை is measured by self-command.
428 calls fearing what should be feared the act of the wise. 905 shows the matching error: the fear here lands on doing good, which ought not be feared.

909 says the man who serves a woman's will loses pleasure with everything else. 1107 compares a beloved's embrace to eating one's own share in one's own home, which suggests that the pleasure 909 says is lost belongs to someone still his own master.

position: நயன் is their conduct, examined so that one can leave them.
quote: ஒழுகலாற்றினை ஆராய்ந்தறிந்து அவரைப் பொருந்தாது விடுக.

position: நயன் is the pleasure they offer, which on examination is not worth approaching.
quote: இன்பத்தை யாராய்ந்து பார்த்து, அவரைச் சாராதொழிக

position: The image describes her inner state: outwardly embracing, inwardly recoiling for the sake of money, like a paid corpse-bearer.
quote: அகத்தால் அருவராநின்றும் பொருள் நோக்கிப் புறத்தால் தழுவுவர்

position: She embraces someone for money and acts out false love.
quote: பணத்துக்காக மட்டுமே ஒருவரைத் தழுவிப் பொய்யன்பு காட்டி நடிப்பது

position: அருட்பொருள் is wealth joined to grace: the wise still pursue wealth, but examine how to use it graciously.
quote: அருளொடு கூடிய பொருளை ஆராய்ந்து செய்யும் அறிவினையுடையார்

position: அருட்பொருள் treats grace itself as the wealth one seeks.
quote: அருளைப் பொருளாக ஆராயும் அறிவுடையார்

position: அணங்கு is a divine woman who takes life through desire, so the embrace is sweet and then fatal.
quote: காமநெறியான் உயிர் கொள்ளும் தெய்வமகள்.

position: அணங்கு simply means affliction, with no divine being.
quote: வருத்தமாமென்று சொல்லுவர்

position: These companions are signs by which one can tell that the goddess has already abandoned a man.
quote: திரு நீக்கிப் பட்டமை இக்குறிகளான் அறியப்படும்

position: Consorting with them is what causes life's distinction to depart.
quote: தொடர்பு கொண்டு உழல்வோரை விட்டு வாழ்வில் அமைய வேண்டிய சிறப்பு அகன்றுவிடும்.

note: 91 defines இன்சொல் as speech soaked in love and free of guile. 911 shows what is left when love is removed: the same sweetness becomes the instrument of harm. So the Kural's praise of sweet speech was never about sweetness alone.

241 ranks the wealth of grace above material wealth, which even the பூரியார் have. 914 applies the same contrast to choice of company, and 919's பூரியர் are the ones who sink, so these verses share a vocabulary of grace against base wealth.

Both tie a man's நலம் to whose shoulders he doesn't touch, using the same verb தோய். 149 says it of another's wife and 916 of women who sell themselves, so the two forbidden categories are treated in one idiom of self-possession.
Fortune as a goddess who leaves or stays: 617 places her at the feet of the unidle man, and 920 says the ones she has dropped can be known by their company.

position: கையறியாமை is helpless not-knowing what to do, itself the fruit of former deeds.
quote: அவன் பழவினைப் பயனாய செய்வதறியாமையைத் தனக்குக் காரணமாக உடைத்து.

position: கையறியாமை is simply not seeing what benefit results.
quote: பயன் அறியாமை யுடைத்து

position: It is indescribable stupidity, with no deed or fruit involved.
quote: விவரிக்கவே முடியாத மூடத்தனமாகும்.

position: This is an analogy. Sleepers differ from the dead yet lack awareness just as they do; drinkers differ from poison-eaters yet lack awareness permanently. He rejects a rival crosswise pairing.
quote: கள்ளுண்பார் நஞ்சுண்பாரின் வேறாதல் உடையரேனும், எக்காலத்தும் அறிவின்மையான் வேறு எனப்பட்டார்

position: Drinkers and poison-eaters are the same, and therefore the drinker's sleep is the same as death.
quote: மது அருந்துவோர்க்கும் நஞ்சு அருந்துவோர்க்கும் வேறுபாடு கிடையாது

position: The speaker is a secret drinker claiming sobriety when not drinking; as soon as he drinks, the hidden fault comes out larger.
quote: மறைந்துண்டு வைத்து யான் கள்ளுண்டறியேன் என்று உண்ணாத பொழுது தம் ஒழுக்கங் கூறுதலையொழிக

position: The speaker claims drink does not intoxicate him; drink itself makes the tongue slip and reveal the hidden things of the mind.
quote: கள்ளுண்டால் களித்தறியே னென்பதனைக் கைவிடுக

position: துரீஇ is searching with a lamp: as light doesn't enter water, so reason doesn't enter his mind.
quote: நீருள் மூழ்கினான் ஒருவனைப் பிறனொருவன் விளக்கினல் நாடுதலை யொக்கும்.

position: துரீஇ is burning him with fire: a submerged man can't be touched by it.
quote: நீரின் கீழே முழுகினானைத் தீயினாற் சுட்டது போலும்

note: 926 says that drinkers are eating poison. 1201 says love is sweeter than liquor because it delights even in memory, taking liquor's delight as the benchmark. The book of love borrows, without judging, the pleasure that this chapter condemns.

Both compare sleep to death. 339 makes this a serious claim about mortality, with waking as birth, and 926 only uses it as a pointer to lost awareness. The commonplace serves metaphysics in one and a warning in the other.

Both place a mother and the worthy in a single scene. In 69 her joy peaks when her son is called சான்றோன்; in 923 his drunkenness pains her and is unthinkable before those same people. Read together, 923 is 69 undone.
Other people's reasons can't reach a drunk (929), but his own sober reflection might (930). The chapter separates argument from self-recognition as means of change.

position: அகடு is the belly: they go hungry here, and suffer hell in the next world.
quote: இம்மைக்கண் வயிறாரப் பெறார்; மறுமைக்கண் நிரயத் துன்பம் உழப்பர்.

position: அகடு is what lies within, the senses and the mind, which are never satisfied, and the covering hides their good qualities.
quote: தமக்கு உள்ளாகிய இந்திரியங்களும் மனமும் இன்புற்று நிறை யப்பெறார்

position: காலை means the time set apart for virtue, wealth and pleasure, especially a king's.
quote: அறம் பொருள் இன்பங்கட்கு அடைத்த காலம் அரசனுக்குச் சூதாடு களத்தின்கண் கழியுமாயின்

position: காலை means the morning hour.
quote: சூது கழகத்தின்கண்ணே காலைப்பொழுது புகுவானாயின்

position: The soul's love is for the body, through which it suffers; as the one quitting gambling is admired, so is the soul that spurns the body.
quote: சூதினை வெறுத்து ஒழிவானை யொக்கும் உடம்பினை வெறுத்தொழியும் உயிர்

position: The love is for life itself, which grows as the body suffers; no renunciation is implied.
quote: உடலுக்குத் துன்பம் தொடர்ந்து வரவர உயிர்மீது கொள்ளுகிற ஆசையும்

note: Under Parimelazhagar's reading of 940 the two are one argument: the soul clings to the body through suffering as a gambler clings through loss, and 345 says that for those ending birth even the body is one attachment too many. 940 is the disease and 345 the cure.

Both use முகடி, the goddess of misfortune. 617 lodges her in idleness and 936 equates her with gambling. Parimelazhagar's remark on 936 that her name is too ill-omened to say makes gambling her acceptable alias.
The hook's bait in 931 becomes the mechanism in 932: the one small win pulls the hundred losses after it. Parimelazhagar explicitly ties them together with அத்தூண்டிற் பொன்.

position: What exceeds or falls short is food and activity, relative to one's constitution, and that disturbs the three.
quote: உணவும் செயல்களும் ஒருவன் பகுதிக்கு ஒத்த அளவின் அன்றி

position: What exceeds or falls short is food, sleep and sexual union.
quote: உணவும் உறக்கமும் இணைவிழைச்சும் தன்னுடம்பின் அளவிற்கு மிகினும் குறையினும்

position: What exceeds or falls short is the three humours themselves.
quote: மூன்றில் ஒன்று அளவுக்கு அதிகமானாலும் குறைந்தாலும் நோய் உண்டாகும்.

position: மறுத்து means refusing the amount the heart wants and stopping at what brings no disease.
quote: தன் உள்ளம் வேண்டிய அளவினான் அன்றிப் பிணிவாரா அளவினால்

position: He takes it as eating by setting aside the food, with incompatibility illustrated by a compensating food.
quote: சுவையும் வீரியமும் மாறுபாடில்லாத உணவை நீக்கி யுண்ப னாயின்

position: உழைச்செல்வான் is the compounder, and each of the four has four sub-qualities of its own.
quote: நான்கு பகுதியையுடைய நான்கு திறத்தது

position: உழைச்செல்வான் is one who stands by to help, and treatment simply has four parts.
quote: அருகிருந்து துணைபுரிபவர் என மருத்துவமுறை நான்கு வகையாக அமைந்துள்ளது.

note: 943 teaches how to carry the body far. 968 asks whether keeping the flesh alive is 'medicine' when dignity has been destroyed. The health chapter treats long life as the aim, and the honour chapter, two away, makes it conditional.
The verses value the same body differently. 943's man has received a body and should carry it far, and 345's renouncer finds it one attachment too many.

A physician and a ruler think in the same form: 949 weighs patient, illness and time before acting, and 471 weighs the deed, oneself, the opponent and allies. Both end in the same verb of action (செயல்), and both reject a universal prescription.

Both use fire for the belly. 947's fire is a measure to observe, and 227's is the disease of hunger that won't touch one who shares food. One is the eater's problem and the other's cure is ethical, which widens what 'not falling ill' means.

950 divides medicine into four roles. 1102 says that other illnesses have other remedies, but the bejewelled woman is herself the remedy for the illness she causes, which collapses the roles of 950 into one.

position: Birth decides: others can be taught these qualities but won't keep them for long.
quote: பிறர்க்காயின் கற்பித்த வழியும் நெடிது நில்லா

position: Conduct defines birth: only those with these qualities can be regarded as high-born.
quote: மற்றவர்களை உயர்ந்த குடியில் பிறந்தவர்களாகக் கருத முடியாது.

position: யார்க்கும் means everyone who is due deference, such as priests, the worthy, ascetics and parents, shown by rising and going to meet them.
quote: பணியப்படுவார் யாவர் மாட்டும் பணிதலை வேண்டுக

position: யார்க்கும் means all people without limit.
quote: யாவர்மாட்டும் தாழ்ந் தொழுகுதலை விரும்புக

note: 951 says that integrity and shame come naturally only to the well-born. 972 says birth is alike for all beings and distinction arises from deeds. This is the Kural's sharpest internal disagreement on lineage, and Kalaignar's reversal of 951 can be read as an attempt to harmonize it with 972.

957 makes the moon's spot the emblem of a visible fault. 1117 asks whether the woman's face, like the moon, carries a spot, and implies it doesn't. The same mark serves moral exposure in one book and the lover's denial of imperfection in another.

In 91 sweet speech comes from a love-soaked and guileless mind. 959 uses speech as a sign of what lies underneath, as the sprout shows the soil. Together they make speech a surface that discloses the source.

223 says that giving before a poor man can utter 'I have nothing' is found only in the well-born. 955 takes the giver's own means shrinking, and holds his nature constant. Giving is the chapter's real measure of lineage in both.
133 says conduct itself is lineage and lapse is low birth. 958 is less radical, since lapse leads people to doubt a man's birth, which keeps birth as the underlying fact while 133 dissolves it.

position: The acts are ones whose omission would mean death, and they must still be refused.
quote: 'இறப்பவரும் வழி இளிவந்தன செய்தாயினும் உய்க' என்னும் வடநூல் முறையை மறுத்து

position: What is given up is wealth and pleasure that would reduce one's nature, however great the amount.
quote: இது பொருளும் இன்பமும் மிகினும், தன்மை குறைவன் செய்யற்க

position: They are obligatory actions, to be avoided if they lessen one's dignity; death is not raised.
quote: கட்டாயமாகச் செய்து தீர வேண்டிய செயல்கள் என்றாலும்கூட

position: Heaven is a real reward that this conduct fails to gain.
quote: ஏனைப் புத்தேளுலகத்துச் செலுத்தாது

position: Heaven is non-existent, and the line asks rhetorically whether it could be obtained this way.
quote: இல்லாத சொர்க்கமா கிடைக்கும்?

position: மானம் வரின் means the point at which honour is won by giving up life.
quote: உயிர் நீக்கத்தான் மானம் எய்தும் எல்லை வரின்

position: மானம் வரின் means when honour is about to be destroyed.
quote: மான முடையார், மானம் அழியவரின் உயிர்விடுவர்

note: 131 says that conduct must be guarded above life. 969 and 970 turn that ranking into an actual death, and show what the abstract comparison costs.

961 gives up even what is indispensable if it would lower one. 1028 warns that a man who is idle and stands on honour will destroy the family he should be building. Honour is the highest thing in one chapter and a hazard in another.

Hair appears at both ends of a value scale in the same chapter. Fallen hair is the worthless thing that a degraded person becomes, and the yak's one lost hair is what can't be survived. The first image is about how others see you, the second about how you see yourself.

Both look at a death through those left behind. 780's soldier dies so that his patron's eyes fill and such death is worth begging for, and 970's man of honour is worshipped by the world. Honour and the warrior ethic share one structure.
125 says bowing is good for all and an added wealth for the rich. 963 keeps the second half and reverses the first for the poor: they are told to stand tall, not to bow.

position: Birth is alike only in being embodied through karma; the work that tests greatness itself differs by varna and individual.
quote: தொழிற்பாகுபாடுகள் வருணந்தோறும் யாக்கைதோறும் வேறுபடுதலின்

position: Greatness simply can't be recognized by lineage.
quote: பெருமையாவது குலத்தினால் அறியப்படா தென்பதூஉம்

position: All are equal by birth, and difference appears only in the skill shown at one's work.
quote: பிறப்பினால் அனைவரும் சமம்.

position: They don't seek to serve the great and acquire their nature, since those proud of birth, wealth or learning think they already have it.
quote: பெரியாரை வழிபட்டு அவர் இயல்பினையாம் கோடும்

position: They don't seek to take the great as support, so having great men as allies is itself greatness.
quote: இது பெரியாரைப் பெறுதலும் பெருமையென்று கூறிற்று.

note: 56 gives the wife's self-guarding, தற்காத்து, as what makes a woman. 974 makes the same self-holding the condition of greatness in anyone. A gendered virtue is universalized, and the phrasing reaches back across the book of virtue.

409 uses மேல் and கீழ் of birth, and ranks the unlearned high-born below the learned low-born. 973 uses the same words of position and wealth. Between them, the Kural detaches worth from both axes of hierarchy.

26, in the chapter on renunciants, defines the great as those who do what is hard. 975 repeats that in the book of wealth, with no renunciation. Parimelazhagar himself cites 26 at 971, so this standard crosses from ascetic to householder.
443 calls cherishing the great and making them one's own the rarest of rare things, using the same பேணி. 976 explains why it is rare: the small don't even conceive of it.
595 says a person's height is as great as their will, as a lotus stem rises with the water. 971 calls that will one's wealth and radiance. Both make aspiration the measure of a person.
Consecutive chapters end up in the same place: 980 ends the chapter on greatness with covering faults, and 984 makes not telling others' faults the defining quality of the worthy.

position: கடன் means what is natural: all good qualities are inherent, otherwise the word சான்றாண்மை wouldn't apply.
quote: நல்லனவாய குணங்கள் எல்லாம் இயல்பாயிருக்கும்

position: கடன் means duty, and all efforts made to fulfil it count as good duties.
quote: நல்ல கடமைகள் என்றே கொள்ளப்படும்.

position: ஆழி means shore: worth is the sea, and they are what holds it in when other seas overflow.
quote: சால்புடைமையாகிய கடற்குக் கரை என்று சொல்லப்படுவார்

position: ஆழி means sea: they stand as the sea that doesn't change when all seas are overturned.
quote: தம்நிலை மாறாத கடலாகத் திகழ்வார்கள்.

note: Chapters 97 and 99 give different answers to humiliation. 967 prefers being called dead to living behind those who scorn you, and 986 makes accepting defeat even from lesser people the touchstone of worth. The two make most sense as distinct ideals, honour and fullness of character, and not as one code.

988 says poverty brings no disgrace to one with worth. 1044 says poverty produces degraded speech even in the well-born. Whether character can hold against poverty is answered one way here and the other in the chapter on poverty.

151 holds up the earth, bearing those who dig it, as the model of forbearance for people. 990 reverses the dependence: the earth's own bearing relies on the worthy. The model has become the dependent.
Two images of bearing a load form a stack: five qualities are pillars carrying worth, and worth carries what the earth bears. The chapter's architecture rests the world on small daily dispositions.
The formula ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் recurs. In 225 this strength is enduring hunger, ranked below relieving it, and in 985 it is bowing. The Kural keeps redefining strength as some form of restraint.
314 says one punishes those who harm by doing them good until they are ashamed, and 987 makes that same return a test of whether worth has any use. 314 gives it a purpose, and 987 makes it a measure.
261 defines austerity as enduring pain and not hurting living things. 984 picks out not killing as its core, in order to place not speaking of others' faults at the same rank for worth.

position: The issue is likeness to good people: bodily likeness doesn't amount to that, because the body doesn't last and character does.
quote: செறியத்தகாத உடம்பால் ஒத்தல் ஒருவனுக்கு நன்மக்களோடு ஒப்பாகாமையின்

position: The issue is membership of humankind: those without good character shouldn't be counted as people.
quote: நற்பண்புகளால் ஒத்திருப்பவர்களே மக்கள் எனப்படுவர்.

note: The same three words meet. 871 calls enmity the thing that has no பண்பு, not to be wanted even in jest. 995 says that those who know others' feelings have பண்பு even within enmity. Enmity is by definition devoid of courtesy, and yet courtesy can survive inside it.
993 says that likeness of limbs isn't human likeness, and 1071 gives the unsettling result: the base look exactly like people. The chapter on baseness starts where this verse ends.
Both call a person a tree for a moral lack: 997 for lacking human courtesy, 576 for having eyes without kindly regard. Each states a difference between being human and being merely alive.

Consecutive chapters end by making the world depend on a moral elite: if the worthy decline the earth can't carry its load (990), and without the courteous the world sinks into it (996). Two images of ground failing.

Both judge wealth by where it lands. In 216 wealth in the hands of the kind is a fruit tree in the village, and in 1000 wealth in the discourteous spoils in its vessel. The next chapter's 1008 completes the set with a poisonous tree.

972 denies that birth settles distinction, and 992, two chapters later, places birth among courtesy's two sources. Parimelazhagar's gloss, which turns birth into conduct, can be seen as a way of closing the gap.
386 says that the land extols a king easy to see and not harsh in speech. 991 gives ordinary people the same recipe. Accessibility is a virtue at every scale in the Kural.

786 distinguishes the laugh of the face from the laugh of the heart in friendship. Parimelazhagar takes 999's laughter as inner joy in others' company, so a failure of that capacity darkens the world and not merely a friendship.

position: The man who does not use it is himself dead, and has nothing further to do with it.
quote: அதனை நுகரானாயின், செத்தான்; அவன் பின்பு செய்யக்கிடந்தது யாது மில்லை.

position: An alternative he allows: once dead, one has no right over it, so enjoy it as soon as it comes.
quote: வையாது பெற்றபொழுதே நுகர்க

position: It is about a literal death: what good is the wealth to one who dies without enjoying it?
quote: அதனை அனுபவிக்காமல் செத்துப்போகிறவனுக்கு.

position: It means rebirth as a ghost that hungers amid food, matching those who watched others' hunger amid plenty.
quote: நிறைதலில்லாத பேய்ப்பிறப்பு உண்டாம்.

position: It describes a person: he becomes a low being with no distinction, with no rebirth involved.
quote: எந்தச் சிறப்புமில்லாத இழி பிறவியாவான்.

position: The man is a disease of the wealth, which could have done both things.
quote: இரண்டும் செய்தற்கு இடனுடைத்தாய செல்வத்திற்கு ஒரு நோய்.

position: The great wealth obtained by such a person is itself faulty.
quote: பெற்ற பெருஞ் செல்வம் குற்றமுடைத்து

position: சிறுதுனி is brief poverty: those who gave everything soon recover, like a cloud. He rejects the other reading as not suited to this chapter.
quote: நிற்கும் காலம் சிறிதாய வறுமை

position: சிறுதுனி is slight displeasure that stops their giving, and the world suffers as with failed rain.
quote: சீருடைய செல்வர் சிறுதுனியால் ஈயாதொழிதல், மாரி பெய் யாமை மிக்காற் போலும்

note: An exact counter-image. 216: wealth in the hands of the kind is a useful tree fruiting in the village. 1008: wealth in the hands of the unwanted is a poison tree fruiting mid-town. Same setting, same act of fruiting, and the holder's character decides whether it feeds or kills.
214 places one who doesn't do what's fitting 'among the dead', and 1001 calls one who won't use his wealth 'dead'. Both use death as a civil status, assigned for failure to circulate wealth.

211 says that duty seeks no return, as with rain. 1010 extends the identification of generous wealth with rain: even their failures are like clouds running dry. The comparison is a consistent one in the Kural.

அடுக்கிய கோடி recurs. For the well-born in 954, stacked crores cannot buy a lowering act. For the miser in 1005, they amount to nothing. The same sum measures character in one and its absence in the other.

570 says that a harsh sceptre over the unlearned is the only burden on the earth. 1003 uses the same phrase for hoarders. The same claim to being earth's one burden is made against a tyrant and against a hoarder.
233 says nothing is imperishable but high fame, and 1004 asks what the unwanted hoarder imagines will remain. Parimelazhagar's note supplies the link: fame rests only on the giver.

position: The women are honoured family women, and he rejects explicitly the reading that they are courtesans.
quote: அழகிய நுதலினையுடைய குலமகளிர் நாண்கள்.

position: They are courtesans, good only in their brow, so that any other shame is merely like theirs.
quote: அழகிய நுதலினாலே நல்லாராகிய கணிகையர் நாணத்தோ டொக்கும்.

position: ஊன் is the body: worth can't have effect without shame, as a soul can't without a body. He reports ஊண் as a variant.
quote: உயிர் உடம்பொடு கூடியல்லது பயனெய்தாத வாறுபோலச் சால்பு நாணோடு கூடியல்லது பயன் எய்தாது

position: The word is food: living things want food above all, and worth wants shame above all.
quote: பலவகை உயிரும் மேற்கூறிய எல்லாவற்றினும் உண்டியைக் கருதிற்று

note: 1017 says the shame-bearing would give up life before shame. 1251 says that love's axe breaks the door barred by shame. The same supreme barrier falls in the book of love, and the whole book of love depends on that collapse.

A nearly identical ranking is made for two virtues. 969 gives up life for மானம் and 1017 for நாண். Kalaignar's gloss of 1017 even uses மானம். The verses suggest honour and shame are the outward and inward faces of a single conviction.
Shame is ornament in both. 1014 calls it the ornament of the worthy, and 1089 asks what other ornaments a woman with shame could need. The same figure crosses gender and books.

315 asks what good knowledge is if one doesn't treat another's pain as one's own. 1015 makes the same move for disgrace: treating another's blame as one's own. Both make moral identification the test of the higher quality.
Both first state what is common to all life, and then find சிறப்பு. For 972 that is deeds, and for 1012 it is shame. Read together, the Kural's account of human distinction becomes specific.
The soul's hold on the body is the simile for virtue's bond in both: in 73 love's tie is like that of life to bone, and in 1013 worth holds on to shame in the same way.

Wood is used twice for those without inner quality. The courtesy chapter's man is a tree in 997, and the shameless man here a wooden puppet. The puppet is worse, since it has been shaped to look alive.

Personified moral forces flee from the faulty. In 924, Shame the good woman turns her back on the drunk, and in 1018 Virtue herself blushes and departs from one who doesn't blush. Shame is first the one who flees and then the condition for virtue's staying.

position: குடி is one's own family, and it rises.
quote: ஒருவன் குடி உயரும்.

position: குடி is the people attached to him, whose pride rises.
quote: அவனைச் சேர்ந்துள்ள குடிமக்களின் பெருமை உயரும்.

position: The deity is said to lead, and leading is an act ascribed to destiny (நியதி).
quote: முன் நடப்பார் செயல் நியதிமேல் ஏற்பட்டது.

position: What is called divine action is the power of nature.
quote: தெய்வச் செயல் எனக்கூறப்படும் இயற்கையின் ஆற்றல்கூட

position: மானம் is the pride of asking 'why must I alone suffer while the rest are comfortable?'
quote: 'இக்குடியிலுள்ளார் யாவரும் இன்பமுற இக்காலத்துத் துன்பமுறுவேன் யானோ?'

position: It is being shaken by degrading attacks made on oneself.
quote: தன்மீது நடத்தப்படும் இழிவான தாக்குதலைக் கண்டு கலங்கினாலோ

position: மறைத்தல் is shielding, as with a shield against spears: he protects them from the three kinds of suffering.
quote: மூவகைத் துன்பமும் உறற்பாலதாய தன் குடியை அவை உறாமற்காக்க முயல்வானது உடம்பு

position: மறைத்தல் is concealing the failings found among kin.
quote: சுற்றத்தார் மாட்டு உளதாகிய குறையை மறைக்கக் கருதுவான் உடம்பு

note: The same words appear with opposite force. In 380 fate comes first (தான்முந் துறும்), defeating whatever one devises (சூழினும்). In 1023 the divine comes first (தான்முந் துறும்) for the one who resolves, and 1024 adds that the end comes without deliberating (சூழாமல்). Priority over human planning works against effort in one and for it in the other.
619 says that effort pays even when the divine doesn't help. 1023 takes up the other case: effort draws the divine to help. Together they cover both options and in each effort wins.

467 says deliberate and then resolve, and that deliberating afterwards is a fault. 1024 says that for those who work without delay for their people, the outcome comes without deliberating. The two can be reconciled only by treating family work as a special case.
Both use the same play on சுற்றம் and சுற்றுதல். In 525 giving and sweet speech surround one with layers of kin, and 1025 extends this until the whole world gathers around as kin.
148's பேராண்மை is not looking at another's wife, and 1026's நல்லாண்மை is ruling one's house. The Kural keeps coining compound forms of manliness that exclude combat, as Parimelazhagar notes here.

481 says that a king needs the right time, like a crow beating an owl by day. Parimelazhagar explicitly cites 481 at 1028 to mark the exception: one who raises his family needs no season. Timing is wisdom for conquest but an excuse for duty.
Under Manakkudavar's reading of 1029 the two use the same verb, மறைத்தல்: greatness hides others' weakness, and so does the family's support. He bears the cost in his body.
Both see the body as a place for suffering to land: a target in 627 and a vessel in 1029. For 627 this insight is what frees one from distress, and for 1029 the suffering is chosen on others' behalf.

position: The rest bow to other patrons and live on what they are given.
quote: பிறரைத் தொழுது, அவர் சில கொடுப்பத் தம் உயிரோம்பி

position: The rest bow to the farmers themselves.
quote: மற்றவர்கள் அவர்களைத் தொழுதுண்டு வாழ வேண்டியிருக்கிறது.

position: The umbrella is that of their king, whose conquests their grain makes possible.
quote: பலவேந்தர் - குடை நிழலதாய மண் முழுதினையும் தம் வேந்தர்குடைக்கீழே காண்பர்.

position: Farmers themselves have the strength to bring all governments under them.
quote: தமது குடைநிழலின் கீழ் கொண்டு வரும் வலிமை பெற்றவர்கள் உழவர்கள்.

note: The same earth responds in two ways. In 151 it supports even those who dig into it, the model of patience. In 1040 it laughs at those who won't dig. Being dug is what it tolerates and even wants, so the virtue chapter's image becomes a joke on the idle.
'X என்னும் நல்லாள்' is a shared formula. Shame the good woman turns her back on the drunk, and Land the good woman laughs at the idle. Both personified women judge men.
ஊடல் is love's sweet sulk in 1330, delightful when embrace follows. 1039 borrows the word to warn an absent owner: the land, like a spouse, wants presence, and here the sulk costs him the harvest.
42 makes the householder the support of renouncers, and 1036 sets the farmer a level below, as the support of renouncing itself. The chain of dependence runs lower than the book of virtue showed.

1065 says even thin gruel earned by one's own effort is the sweetest thing. 1033 makes that a social claim: only those who eat from their own ploughing truly live. The chapters on begging supply this chapter's value.
1051 tells one to ask of those worth asking and makes refusal their fault, not yours. 1035 presents a person who never needs the permission, and who is on the giving end of that same act.

position: தோல் means graceful speech, as Tolkappiyam uses it, and he rejects reading it as the body.
quote: பழைய குடிவரவினையும் அதற்கு ஏற்ற சொல்லினையும் ஒருங்கே கெடுக்கும்.

position: தோல் means beauty of form.
quote: குடிப்பிறப்பினையும் வடிவழகினையும் ஒருங்கு கெடுக்கும்

position: தோல் means fame, and the desire is a greed that poverty causes.
quote: பரம்பரைப் பெருமையையும், புகழையும் ஒரு சேரக் கெடுத்துவிடும்.

position: அறஞ்சாரா describes the poverty: it doesn't come from virtue nor yield virtue.
quote: காரண காரியங்களுள் ஒன்றானும் இயையாமை.

position: It describes the man, who has left the path of virtue because of poverty.
quote: அறநெறியிலிருந்து விலகி நிற்பவனை

position: To renounce fully is to give up the body itself, for honour's sake; those left by kin have done everything else.
quote: நின்ற தம் உடம்பினையும் துறத்தல்.

position: It is to give up attachment to wealth, which brings pleasure to the poor.
quote: இது துறப்பாராயின், இன்ப முறலா மென்று கூறிற்று.

note: 423 says the mark of understanding is seeing the truth whoever says it. 1046 reports that a poor man's meaning falls flat however true it is. One gives the ideal, and the other the way the world listens.

959 says that speech reveals lineage as a sprout reveals soil. 1044 shows the signal failing: poverty brings degraded speech out of the well-born. Speech is a sign of poverty as well as lineage, so the test is less reliable than chapter 96 claims.

368 says there is no suffering for those without desire. 1043 makes poverty itself into desire, which Parimelazhagar glosses as: without craving there's no poverty. An ascetic insight enters the chapter on economic misery, while the rest of the chapter denies it.

378 says that the destitute would renounce if what they must suffer would pass. 1050, with the same துப்புரவு இல்லார், tells them to do it. The verse of fate explains why it doesn't happen, while this verse only mocks them for it.
247 keeps two forms of lack apart: no grace loses the next world, no wealth loses this one. 1042 collapses them: poverty takes both worlds. Grace alone turns out not to secure the next world.
'X என ஒரு பாவி' appears in both. Envy is the sinner in 168 and poverty in 1042, with both sending one down. Parimelazhagar links them himself. The state of being poor gets the same grammar as a vice.

The mother marks a moral limit twice. Her pain at drunkenness (923) still has love in it, because she's the most forgiving audience, and poverty does what drink couldn't by making her look at her son as a stranger.

position: The suffering is the asker's: the courting, reading the giver's moods and being refused, which is spared if the giver anticipates.
quote: அவையுறாமல் வருதலாவது, அவர் முன்னுணர்ந்து ஈயக்கோடல்.

position: The suffering is that of both, giver and receiver.
quote: வழங்குபவர், வாங்குபவர் ஆகிய இருவர் மனத்திற்கும் துன்பம் எதுவுமின்றி

position: கடன் is honour, and it is the asker's: he reads 963 to explain why such a giver can sense a poor person's dignity.
quote: கரத்தல் இல்லாத நெஞ்சினையுடைய மானம் அறிவார்

position: கடன் is social obligation, the duty of helping.
quote: கரப்பிலாத நெஞ்சினை யுடைய ஒப்புரவறிவார்

position: கடன் is the giver's sense of duty.
quote: உள்ளதை ஒளிக்காத உள்ளமும், கடமையுணர்வும் கொண்டவரிடத்தில்

position: Without someone to give to, others would earn no fame or merit, and they might as well be lifeless.
quote: அவர்க்கு ஈதலைச் செய்து புகழும் புண்ணியமும் எய்தாமையின், உயிருடையரல்லார்

position: Asking and giving are the order of the world, so asking shouldn't be treated as low.
quote: இரத்தலும் ஈதலும் உலகியல்பாதலான், இரத்தல் இழிவென்று கொள்ளப்படா

position: He changes the subject: those who won't let askers near are the puppets.
quote: தம்மை நெருங்கக் கூடாது என்கிற மனிதர்களுக்கும்

note: Consecutive chapters open in direct opposition. 1051: ask if you find those worth asking. 1061: not asking, even of those who give gladly and are as dear as eyes, is ten million times better. Parimelazhagar's solution makes 1051 apply only at the edge of death; the verses themselves don't state this.

The wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை) marks a lack of real life in both. In 1020 it's a person without shame, and in 1058 a world without askers. Each chapter finds what makes movement into life, one in an inner quality and one in a social transaction.

232 says that all that speakers praise rests on those who give to askers. 1059 makes the dependence explicit: the fame needs the asker as well. The asker turns out to be necessary for a fame that seemed the giver's alone.

Asking from the right person is like giving (1054), yet asking even water for a cow is the most degrading thing the tongue can do (1066). The chapters give opposite values to one act, and the difference of giver doesn't fully explain it, since 1061 refuses even the best givers.
Parimelazhagar himself cites 963 here: the poor must stand tall, and asking without speaking lets them do so. The honour chapter's demand shapes how begging can be done at all.

position: The creator decrees each being's livelihood along with its karma at conception; if that includes begging, the evil returns on him and he should suffer the same.
quote: சில உயிர்க்கு இரத்தலையும் ஒரு செய் தொழிலாகக் கற்பித்தானாயின், அத்தீவினையால் தானும் அத்துன்பமுறல் வேண்டும்

position: The verse is about those who choose to beg to survive; the conclusion is that death is better than begging.
quote: இஃது இரக்கு மதனின், இறத்தல் அமையு மென்றது.

position: He distances himself from the idea: it is whoever is 'said' to have created the world.
quote: உலகத்தைப் படைத்தவனாகச் சொல்லப்படுபவனும் கெட்டொழிந்து திரியட்டும்.

position: The melting heart is that of an onlooker who imagines the cruelty; he notes that all others say it's the asker's.
quote: இதற்குப் பிறரெல்லாம் 'இரக்கின்றவர் உள்ளம் உருகும்' என்று உரைத்தார்.

position: It concerns the asker, who has nothing to gain.
quote: இஃது இரப்பார்க்கு ஆக்கமில்லை என்றது.

note: 377 says that even those with crores enjoy only as the apportioner apportioned. 1062 curses that very apportioner, if the portion includes begging. The chapter on fate accepts the apportioning, and this chapter refuses it, and Parimelazhagar's gloss makes the two nearly the same figure.

Gruel is sweeter than ambrosia twice. 64: when one's child's little hand has stirred it. 1065, in Parimelazhagar's reading: when one's own effort earned it. The two supply the Kural's two sources of value in a poor meal, love and independence.

A flimsy vessel breaks up in both. 1134's raft of shame and good manliness is swept away by the flood of love. 1068's boat of asking is split by the rock of concealment. Each shows a failed crossing, but the vessel in 1134 is what one is proud of.
971 calls one's radiance the wealth of aspiration, and 1064 gives its most extreme form. Without means to live, the refusal itself is too large for the world.

position: It is a likeness of body between two different kinds, distinguished only by whether they have good qualities.
quote: மக்கட் சாதிக்கும் கயச்சாதிக்கும் வடிவு ஒத்தலின்

position: It is hypocrisy within one person, who is base while acting good.
quote: குணத்தில் ஒருவர் கயவராக இருப்பார். ஆனால், நல்லவரைப் போலக் காட்டிக் கொள்வார்.

position: These are people who behave as they please like strays, on a smaller scale than the base man, and he boasts by exceeding them.
quote: தன்னிற் சுருங்கிய பட்டியாய் ஒழுகுவாரைக் கண்டானாயின்

position: These are women at home with grace, and the base pride themselves on being more graceful still.
quote: மனையகத்திருந்து பொற்புடையாராகிய பெண்டிரைக் காணின்

position: They invent faults that don't exist, with skill enough to make them believable.
quote: அவர்மாட்டு வடுவில்லையாகவும் உண்டாக்கவல்லனாம்.

position: They search out faults that do exist in such people.
quote: அவர் மாட்டு உள்ள குற்றங்களை ஆராயவல்லாராவர் கயவர்

note: Two responses to the same crisis mark the moral range of the Book of Wealth. When honour or distress comes, those like the yak give up life (969), and the base sell theirs for a price, in haste (1080). The book ends on the second.

A scale of giving. In Parimelazhagar's reading of 1051 the worthiest give before anything is said, in 1078 the worthy give when told, and the base give when crushed. 1077 adds that the base give nothing to any who can't hurt them.
A spy in 587 hears the hidden and knows it without doubt, and in 1076 the base also hear it, but proclaim it. Trading in secrets is a skill or a vice according to whether one can hold them.

368 says there's no suffering for those without desire, the ascetic's freedom from anguish. 1072's base have that freedom, by not knowing what is good. The verse exposes a counterfeit of equanimity: peace of mind can't itself be the measure.

1018 sees shame as the condition of virtue, with virtue itself ashamed to approach the shameless. 1075 is a kind of counter-case: the base still have conduct, with fear and desire in place of shame. Their conduct looks alike and differs in its source.
The same satirical move rises in rank: they're like men, and then they're like gods. What makes them like the gods, acting as they please, is what makes them not like men.

position: அமர்த்தன means the eyes are at odds with her gentle nature; they are cruel where she is not.
quote: அமர்த்தல்: மாறுபடுதல்.

position: The word means the eyes fit her: they suit the girl in the work they do.
quote: அமர்தல் - மேவல்.

position: The eyes are a puzzling contradiction in someone so womanly.
quote: ஏனிந்த மாறுபாடு?

position: The man speaks as he sets out to read her intent.
quote: தலைமகள் குறிப்பறிதல் உற்றான் சொல்லியது.

position: The woman thinks this, pained after seeing the man, which reverses the chapter's point of view.
quote: இது தலைமகள் தலைமகனைக்கண்டுழி வருத்தமுற்றுக் கருதியது.

note: The warrior of 774 pulls a spear from his own body and laughs. The warrior of 1088 has that same reputation and is broken by a forehead. The Kural's courage has no defence against this enemy.

1014 calls modesty the ornament of the great, and without it their proud bearing is a disease. 1089 uses the same idea for a girl's beauty, so the ethical chapter's metaphor returns as a lover's literal claim that jewels are redundant.

Both set love above liquor for delighting through sight. 1090 says it at the first encounter and 1281 says it deep in the relationship, so the comparison holds from the start of love through its maturity.

position: The painful look discloses desire in her mind and the healing look shows her love; he rejects calling the first a neutral look, since one-sided pain wouldn't be mutual love.
quote: நோய் செய்யும் நோக்கு அவள் மனத்தனாய காமக்குறிப்பினை வெளிப்படுத்துகின்ற நோக்கு.

position: The two looks are successive: the first look that hurt him, then a later one mixed with shyness and concern for his pain.
quote: நோய்நோக்கென்பது முதல் நோக்கின நோக்கம்

position: She narrows one eye as she glances; the 'as though' is there because even this isn't openly done.
quote: சிறக்கணித்தல்: சுருங்குதல்.

position: He reads the line as 'at one moment', and the verb as agreeing: she smiles as one who has consented.
quote: ஒருகால் உடம்பட்டாள் போல

position: The harsh speaker is the friend, who is sending him away while really seeking to help; he says this to himself.
quote: தோழி சேண்படுத்தவழி அவள் குறிப்பு அறிந்த தலைமகன் தன்னுள்ளே சொல்லியது.

position: The case is one where the body shows agreement and speech refuses, which is taken as consent.
quote: உறுப்பினாலிசைவுகாட்டி, உரையினால் மறுப்பினும் உடன்படுதலா மென்றது.

position: The harsh speaker is the woman herself, hiding love under a stranger's manner.
quote: அவள் அகத்தில் கோபமின்றி அன்பு கொண்டிருப்பது

position: ஏர் here is the good sign that shows in her smile, a promise that won't fail him after his pleading look.
quote: தோன்றுகின்றதோர் நன்மைக் குறிப்பு உண்டு.

position: ஏர் is beauty, the quality that surpasses her form at that moment.
quote: அழகு - தன்வடிவினுள் மிக்க குணம்

position: The friend, having heard both, speaks in general terms about what she has noticed.
quote: இருவர் சொல்லும் கேட்டு உலகியல்மேல் வைத்துக் கூறியவாறு.

position: The man, about to approach her, speaks to his own heart.
quote: இது சார்தலுறுகின்ற தலைமகன் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

note: Both chapters are named குறிப்பறிதல. In 709, a skilled reader of eyes can tell enmity from friendship in a court. 1097 warns that a lover's eyes can put on enmity while friendly, so the statecraft skill has to work harder here.
In 1091 one look wounds and another heals. In 1102 the woman herself is both the disease and its medicine. The paradox grows from a glance to the whole person once they have united.

position: The world is Vishnu's, reached by ascetics who renounce the senses; he rejects the Indra reading on the ground that lotus-eyed isn't Indra's name.
quote: தாமரைக்கண்ணான் என்பது அவனுக்குப் பெயரன்மையின், அஃது உரையன்மையறிக.

position: The world is Indra's heaven, and the point is that heaven's pleasure is simply this.
quote: இந்திரனது சுவர்க்கம்

position: Her friend has urged marriage, and he declines: this secret union already gives him the reward of the householder's life.
quote: 'இல்லறஞ்செய்தார் எய்தும் துறக்கத்து இன்பம் எனக்கு இப்புணர்ச்சியே தரும்' என வரைவு உடன்படான் கூறியவாறாயிற்று.

position: The woman embraced is already his wife, so the verse describes married pleasure.
quote: தனது அழகிய காதல் மனைவியைத் தழுவுகின்ற இன்பத்துக்கு

position: He agrees in form but declines the marriage she urges, because here there aren't two.
quote: 'ஈண்டு இருவர் இல்லை இன்மையான், இஃது ஒவ்வாது' என்பது கருத்து.

position: This is a dismissal: quarrels belong to married men who stray to courtesans, and a couple as one as they are wants no such 'reward'.
quote: அப்பயன் இருதலைப் புள்ளிள் ஓருயிராய் உழுவலன்புடைய எமக்கு வேண்டா

position: This is delight: the man has just ended her sulk and united with her, and celebrates the sequence.
quote: ஊடற் குறிப்புத் தோன்ற நின்ற தலைமகளை ஊடல் தீர்த்துப் புணர்ந்த தலைமகன்

note: 343 tells the renunciant to destroy the pull of the five senses and give up all desire at once. 1101 celebrates the same five senses meeting their fill in a single person. The Kural gives each its place in different books without reconciling them.

In 1104 he marvels at a fire that burns at a distance and cools up close. In 1159, a voice in separation says ordinary fire can't burn at a distance at all. The same paradox goes from a delighted question to a complaint.
1065 says even thin gruel earned by your own labour is the sweetest food, for the sake of self-respect. 1107 borrows that dignity of one's own table to describe an embrace.

1109 lists the quarrel as love's reward, and the Kural's last verse, 1330, ends the whole work on the same idea. Parimelazhagar's scornful reading of 1109 is hard to square with the fact that 1330 and the final chapters celebrate the sequence.

396 says knowledge wells up in proportion to study, like water in a sand well. 1110 takes the same unlimited knowledge as the measure of desire, except that in love more of it reveals a lack and not a supply.

position: The flowers don't match her eyes, and the heart is rebuked for its false comparison now that he alone has seen them.
quote: அம்மலர்கள் ஒவ்வாமை கண்டு, ஒப்புமை கருதிய நெஞ்சை இகழ்ந்து கூறியவாறு.

position: Her eyes match flowers in colour but not in quality.
quote: கண் பூவினது நிறமொக்குமாயினும்

position: The verse is direct praise: her eyes are indeed a flower that many see and admire.
quote: பலரும் கண்டு வியக்கும் மலராகவே திகழ்கிறது.

position: This is a covert refusal: her friend has proposed elopement, and feet like these couldn't cross the wilderness.
quote: உடன் போக்கு உரைத்த தோழிக்கு அதனது அருமை கூறி மறுத்தது.

position: It is plain praise: her feet are softer than these.
quote: இஃது அவையிற்றினும் மெல்லியது அடியென்று கூறிற்று.

note: 957 uses the moon's spot to say the flaws of the high-born show as conspicuously as a mark on the moon. 1117 uses the same spot in praise of an unblemished face. In one, a mark reveals a failing; in the other, its absence is the point.
The lily in 1114 would bow and look at the ground, as the woman herself does in 1094. The lily is imagined acting out the shame of being outdone, in a gesture she makes for love.
Both disqualify a comparison because it is பலர் காணும், seen by many. What starts as a heart scolded about flowers becomes an instruction to the moon, showing how his praise rests on exclusivity.

Both use the same phrase for the friendship of body and life. In 338 it is like a bird flying from an abandoned shell, an image of how easily it ends. In 1122 it is the lover's image for an unbreakable bond. The thing he swears by is what the book on renunciation calls fragile, and in 1124 he seems to know it.

He says 'I don't know forgetting' with a clever smile. In 1207 the woman uses the same words, மறப்பறியேன், and adds that even remembering burns her. The same claim of constant memory is banter for one and torment for the other.
Here the town's talk is a misunderstanding she can rebut. In 1147, the talk has become manure for the love itself. Her stance towards gossip shifts from defence to using it.

position: உழந்து assumes that he has already enjoyed love and has now lost access to it.
quote: அரியராய மகளிரோடு காமத்தை அனுபவித்துப் பின் அது பெறாது துன்புற்ற ஆடவர்க்கு

position: The word means only striving and suffering because of love, and says nothing of past union.
quote: காமம் காரணமாக முயன்று வருந்தினார்க்கு

position: The man answers the friend's taunt that men ought to endure better: it is the birth of women that has this restraint, and he lacks it.
quote: 'பிறப்பு விசேடத்தால் அவ்வடக்கம் எனக்கு இல்லையாகா நின்றது; நீ அஃது அறிகின்றிலை,' என்பதாம்.

position: The friend tells the man that his beloved suffers just as much, and that women's lot is simply not to ride, to calm his distress.
quote: தலைமகன் ஆற் றாமை நீங்குதற்பொருட்டுத் தோழி கூறியது.

position: The woman speaks, her guarded love having grown; desire isn't afraid of women's firmness, நிறை அரியர்.
quote: 'இவர் நிறையால் நாம் மீதூர்தற்கு அரியர்' என்று அஞ்சுதல் செய்யாது

position: The friend speaks to refuse a daytime meeting because of scandal, and the woman lacks restraint.
quote: இஃது அம்பலம் அலரும் ஆகாவென்று தோழி பகற்குறி மறுத்தது.

note: 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame and never give up shame for life. In 1132, the lover sets shame aside to save his body and life. It reverses the ethic exactly, in a book of its own.

For the man, love's flood carries off the raft he had. For the woman in 1164, there is a sea of love and no raft at all. Her situation is worse than his: she has neither the raft nor his palmyra horse.

54 asks what has greater worth than a woman, provided she has the firmness of chastity, using the same words, பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்க. 1137 gives the worth a specific content: enduring a sea of desire without a public remedy. The praise comes from a man who is announcing that he won't do the same.

position: The man, unable to reach her, is sustained by talk that makes her seem attainable.
quote: அங்ஙனம் அரியாளை எளியளாக்கி எடுக்கின்றமையின், அஃது அவ்வாருயிர்க்குப் பற்றுக்கோடாக நின்றது

position: It is her life that the gossip sustains.
quote: அவளது ஆருயிர் நிற்கும்

position: It is the couple's life, which survives on hope that talk will help their love succeed.
quote: எம் உயிர் போகாமல் இருக்கிறது

position: The man says that his own desire is so strong that gossip itself gives him pleasure.
quote: வேட்கை மிகுதியால் அலரும் இன்பஞ் செய்யாநின்றது என்பதாம்.

position: The friend replies to the man, who has asked whether this gossip is hurting them.
quote: நுமக்குத் துன்பமாயிற்றே இவ்வலரென்று வினாவிய தலைமகற்குத் தோழி கூறியது.

position: தாம் வேண்டின் means 'if we ask', and the friend is steering the man towards elopement, which the gossip now justifies.
quote: இனிக் காதலர்தாமும்யாம் வேண்டியக்கால் அதனை இனிதின் நேர்வர்

position: The words mean 'if the lover also wishes', and his consent depends on his own desire.
quote: காதலரும் விரும்பினால் அதை ஒப்புக் கொள்வார்.

note: 183 says that it is better to die than to live by backbiting, because it is a false kind of life. In 1141 backbiting is what keeps someone else alive. The same act has a very different moral look from the side of its target.
